messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Car Similarity: Similar cars, Crowding: Crowded places
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Face Hiding: cover face with hands

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Voss is a 33-year-old graphic designer of Polish descent who presents following a traumatic encounter with law enforcement approximately fourteen months ago. He is currently divorced and lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a mid-sized American city, where he works primarily from home as a freelance designer. His PCL-5 score of 74 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged over the past year reflects a life substantially reorganised around a single, violent night.

The incident occurred when Aleksander was driving home late from a client meeting. He was pulled over by two officers in an unmarked dark sedan — a vehicle he initially mistook for a private car following him. What began as a routine stop escalated with disorienting speed. One officer yanked his door open before he had finished lowering the window; within seconds Aleksander was on the asphalt, face pressed to the ground, a knee at the back of his neck and his arms wrenched behind him. He could not see what was happening. He could not speak without being told to shut up. The darkness of the road, the weight on his back, the close proximity of other vehicles that had slowed to watch — all of it converged into a prolonged stretch of time in which he was genuinely uncertain whether he would survive. He was eventually released without charge. No explanation was given.

In the weeks that followed, Aleksander noticed that he could not work after sundown. Sitting at his desk in the dark felt intolerable in a way he struggled to name — his body simply refused to stay still, and he would find himself checking the window repeatedly or turning on every light in the apartment. He began leaving lamps on through the night, and when he woke in the dark he described a sensation of the floor rushing up toward him, as though he were back on the asphalt. He had come to believe that darkness itself was a condition under which terrible things happened without warning, and no amount of reasoning had shifted that conviction.

Driving became another site of dread. He had sold his car within two months of the incident, telling himself it was for financial reasons, though he knew that was not the whole truth. What frightened him most was encountering a dark-coloured sedan in traffic — particularly one that appeared to be following behind him — which would trigger an immediate and overwhelming sense that something was about to go catastrophically wrong. He now relies on rideshares, but even as a passenger he will scan the mirrors and track cars that linger near them, certain that proximity to the wrong vehicle means danger.

His work as a graphic designer has been affected in ways that have begun to cost him professionally. A client whose branding project required regular in-person workshops at a busy downtown studio eventually dropped him after Aleksander cancelled three consecutive meetings. Crowded rooms — the kind of collaborative, open-plan creative spaces that define much of his industry — had become unmanageable. The press of bodies, the noise, the sense of being hemmed in recalled the feeling of being surrounded on the road that night, and he would cover his face with his hands or simply leave without explanation.

He had been drinking most evenings since the spring, initially to get through the night hours and then as a way of blunting the edges of days that felt unrelenting. He also kept a supply of over-the-counter sleep aids, though he acknowledged these rarely worked as intended. He took long routes through the city specifically to avoid the police precinct two blocks from his usual grocery store, and had stopped watching any television that might feature officers in uniform, deleting several streaming services rather than risk an unexpected scene.

What finally brought him to seek help was a phone call from his ex-wife, who had heard from a mutual friend that he was not well. She asked him directly whether he was managing, and he found he had no convincing answer. He is most afraid, he says, that what happened has permanently altered something in him — that the person who could work late into the night, who could move freely through the world, is simply gone. What he is hoping for, with a tentativeness that feels fragile, is some evidence that this is not true.
